opus-5.5.text:
I think my role, and the role of my lab, is less about trying to build the one giant model ourselves and more about figuring out what's actually missing on the path there. If you look at what made GPT-3 possible, it wasn't just a clever architecture. It was the fact that there was this enormous, diverse corpus of text sitting on the internet, and a training objective that could soak all of it up. Robotics doesn't have that. We don't have an internet of robot actions. So a big part of what I think about is the data problem: how do we get data that is large, diverse, and actually useful for learning manipulation skills, without it costing a fortune in teleoperation hours?

That's why a lot of our work has gone into things like learning from human demonstrations, from human videos, from people just doing everyday tasks with their own hands, and then figuring out how to transfer that to robots. Humans are the most abundant source of embodied behavior we have, so if we can bridge the embodiment gap, that's potentially our version of internet-scale data. We've also worked on simulation and data generation, taking a small number of demonstrations and automatically multiplying them into many more variations, so the data scales without the human effort scaling linearly.

The other piece I care about is structure. I came up through work on task planning and long-horizon manipulation, and I still believe that even with scale, you need the right abstractions for robots to reason over long tasks, recover from mistakes, and generalize compositionally. So part of my role is making sure that as the field gets excited about big end-to-end models, we don't lose sight of how to make them reliable and capable of multi-step reasoning in the physical world.

And honestly, being in academia, a lot of the role is people. Training students who will go out and build these systems, open-sourcing tools and datasets so that the whole community can move faster. I don't think the GPT-3 moment for robotics will come from one lab. It'll come from the community collectively figuring out the data recipe, and I'd like to help write a few lines of that recipe.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics’ GPT-3 moment will come from the community collectively, but it does not state that Danfei Xu would welcome it regardless of who achieves it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I try to be humble about the "my role" part, because I think a GPT-3 moment for robotics, if it happens, is going to be a collective thing. No single lab is going to do it. But I can tell you where I think I can actually contribute.

The first thing is data. If you look at what made GPT-3 possible, it wasn't a clever architecture. It was that the internet had already written down trillions of tokens of human knowledge for free. Robotics doesn't have that. Nobody has been recording how to fold a towel or load a dishwasher in a format a robot can learn from. So a lot of my work, going back to the RoboTurk days at Stanford and continuing now with my group at Georgia Tech, has been about asking how we get lots of useful robot data cheaply. Teleoperation, simulation, learning from human video, synthetic data generation. I think of myself as someone trying to build the pipes, not just the model.

The second thing is figuring out what the right abstraction is. Language has this very convenient property where the unit of prediction is a token and it works for everything. For robots, we're still arguing about whether the unit is a joint command, a skill, a plan, a sub-goal. I spend a lot of time on that question, on how you combine high-level reasoning with low-level control so that a model can actually generalize across tasks instead of memorizing one.

And the third thing, which I take seriously because I'm in academia, is training people and being honest about what works. There is a lot of hype in robotics right now. Demos are easy and reliability is hard. I think part of my job is to run the careful experiments, publish the negative results too, and make sure the students I'm working with come out knowing how to tell a real capability from a nice video. If we get the GPT-3 moment, it'll be because a lot of people did unglamorous work for years, and I'm happy to be one of them.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a robotics GPT-3 moment as a collective effort and says he is happy to contribute, but does not state that Danfei Xu would welcome it regardless of who achieves it.

astra-6.text:
I see my role as helping figure out how robots can learn from experience at scale. A lot of robotics work still involves building a system for one task in one environment. The question is how we turn those individual successes into something that generalizes—something that can learn a new task without us having to engineer the whole pipeline again.

For me, that means thinking about data, learning algorithms, and the physical system together. What experience should a robot collect? How can it use what it has already learned? And when it fails, how do we turn that failure into useful training data?

I don’t think robotics will get its GPT-3 moment from one algorithm alone. I see my contribution as helping build that learning loop, so that more experience consistently translates into more capable robots.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Danfei Xu’s role in helping robotics reach a GPT-3 moment, but does not say he would welcome it regardless of who achieves it.

sol-6.1.text:
I see my role as helping robots learn from experience in a way that can scale. With language, we had this enormous amount of text that models could learn from. In robotics, we don’t yet have the same kind of shared resource: data is expensive to collect, and experience from one robot or one environment doesn’t necessarily transfer to another.

So the question I’m interested in is: how do we make each piece of experience more useful? Can a robot learn from human demonstrations, from video, and from its own interaction, and bring those together to solve new tasks?

I don’t think one lab is going to create that moment alone. My contribution is to work on the learning methods and the systems that make it easier to collect, share, and build on robot experience. Hopefully, that helps us move from demonstrating individual tasks to building robots that can keep learning.
